elements.id-string-3: Image diffusion has recently shown remarkable performance in image synthesis and implicitly as an image prior.
elements.id-string-4: Such a prior has been used with conditioning to solve the inpainting problem, but only supporting binary user-based conditioning.We derive a fuzzy-conditioned diffusion, where implicit diffusion priors can be exploited with controllable strength.
elements.id-string-5: Our fuzzy conditioning can be applied pixel-wise, enabling the modification of different image components to varying degrees.
elements.id-string-6: Additionally, we propose an application to facial image correction, where we combine our fuzzy-conditioned diffusion with diffusion-derived attention maps.
elements.id-string-7: Our map estimates the degree of anomaly, and we obtain it by projecting on the diffusion space.
elements.id-string-8: We show how our approach also leads to interpretable and autonomous facial image correction.
elements.id-string-10: Image-conditioned diffusion, fuzzy conditioning, diffusion projection, autonomous image correction
elements.id-string-13: Denoising diffusion methods~\cite{sohl2015deep} are effective probabilistic image generation models~\cite{ho2020denoising} that learn to synthesize images by gradually recovering them from noisier distributions.
elements.id-string-14: They have good sample quality due to their pixel-wise operation, for instance compared with variational auto-encoders~\cite{pandey2021vaes,pandey2022diffusevae}, or optimal transport distribution mapping~\cite{daniels2021score}.
elements.id-string-15: Denoising diffusion currently remains an active research topic, with recent work on balancing the advantages of regular and residual latents~\cite{benny2022dynamic} and for balancing the trade-off between diversity and high photorealism~\cite{sehwag2022generating}.
elements.id-string-16: For a more extensive overview, we refer the reader to the survey by Croitoru~\textit{et al.}~\cite{croitoru2022diffusion}.
elements.id-string-17: As image generators, diffusion models implicitly learn image distribution representations that can be exploited in a multitude of applications~\cite{chung2022diffusion}, similar to adversarially trained priors~\cite{el2022bigprior}.
elements.id-string-18: For instance, their implicit prior is useful for image-to-image translation to map across different domains~\cite{sasaki2021unit,saharia2022palette}, for image super-resolution~\cite{saharia2022image}, as well as for synthesizing images with text-based conditioning~\cite{saharia2022photorealistic}.
elements.id-string-19: Their probabilistic nature also enables diverse image completion through randomized sampling~\cite{horita2022structure}.
elements.id-string-20: Stochastic differential equation models were recently used for image editing where the user can control the degree of projection on the perturbed space~\cite{meng2021sdedit}.
elements.id-string-21: A direct inpainting application is presented in~\cite{lugmayr2022repaint}, providing both state-of-the-art results as well as different diverse outputs due to the stochasticity of the diffusion prior.
elements.id-string-22: In contrast, we propose a generalization of inpainting to the non-binary setting, in an effort towards prior contribution control~\cite{el2020blind,el2022bigprior} and control over network hallucination~\cite{el2021deep}.
elements.id-string-23: We present a fuzzy-conditioned diffusion where inpainting is a special case.
elements.id-string-24: Our model can synthesize novel images from different stochastic samples, while conditioning on a given input image in an adjustable way.
elements.id-string-25: The conditioning can be spatially varying and can also be fuzzy (non-binary) in nature.
elements.id-string-26: In other words, the diffusion model can be conditioned on an input image to a varying degree, and this degree can change across the image, thus exploiting the underlying pixel-based formulation of denoising diffusion.
elements.id-string-27: Diffusion models can also be used for out-of-distribution detection~\cite{liu2022diffusion,wyatt2022anoddpm,graham2022denoising}.
elements.id-string-28: The first challenge in out-of-distribution detection is to learn a good image prior for the in-distribution data, which diffusion models can effectively do.
elements.id-string-29: Another challenge is to then classify out-of-distribution test cases.
elements.id-string-30: The approach in~\cite{graham2022denoising}, inspired by previous work using deep auto-encoders~\cite{gong2019memorizing}, classifies test cases based on the full stack of reconstruction errors across a sequence of projections on all latent spaces of a diffusion model.
elements.id-string-31: A second approach proposes a combination of a diffusion reconstruction with a learned discriminator network to obtain the final classification~\cite{liu2022diffusion}.
elements.id-string-32: Another more medically-oriented approach aims to detect and quantify deviations on the pixel-wise level with a non-Gaussian diffusion~\cite{wyatt2022anoddpm}.
elements.id-string-33: Building on these methods, we construct a diffusion projection attention map on a standard denoising diffusion model.
elements.id-string-34: We then exploit this map in our fuzzy-conditioned diffusion to guide an autonomous image correction on a facial image application.
elements.id-string-35: We summarize our contributions as follows.
elements.id-string-36: We derive a novel approach to condition diffusion models on images, such that the conditioning can be spatially varying as well as fuzzy in strength.
elements.id-string-37: This enables both a generalization of inpainting where the degree of hallucination is controlled, and a generalization of image conditioning to be spatially adaptive.
elements.id-string-38: We additionally provide a projection-based anomaly map, enabling our model to perform autonomous face correction.
elements.id-string-40: We exploit diffusion models~\cite{sohl2015deep} to propose a diffusion with a fuzzy image conditioning (Sec.~\ref{sec:fuzzy}) and to obtain a guide-free attention map through projection (Sec.~\ref{sec:projection}), the combination of which is applied for autonomous facial image correction.

elements.id-string-62: The next forward step to obtain $x_t$ is preceded by the following transformation over $x_{t-1}$
elements.id-string-63: \begin{equation} x_m \coloneqq \sqrt{\overbar{\alpha}_{t-1}} x + \frac{ m \cdot x^r_{t-1} + (1-m)\cdot x_{t-1} - \sqrt{\overbar{\alpha}_{t-1}} x }{ \sqrt{1-2\cdot m + 2\cdot m^2} }, \end{equation}
elements.id-string-64: using a fuzzy weight map $m$ that can be obtained from Sec.~\ref{sec:projection} or can be any map of same dimensions as $x$ such as its values are in $[0,1]$.
elements.id-string-65: $x$ is the conditioning input image that becomes the ground-truth target when $m\to 1$ and gets ignored when $m\to 0$.
elements.id-string-66: The standardization coefficient $\sqrt{1-2\cdot m + 2\cdot m^2}$ comes from the fact that the resulting variance at $t-1$  of $x_m$ is given by $m^2 V\{x^r_{t-1}\} + (1-m)^2 V\{x_{t-1}\}$ where both variances $V\{x^r_{t-1}\}$ and $V\{x_{t-1}\}$ are made equivalent by design, matching $(1-\overbar{\alpha}_t)$.
elements.id-string-67: We then obtain $x_t$ by a forward step over $x_m$ instead of over $x_{t-1}$.
elements.id-string-68: Lastly, we use the harmonization resampling technique presented in~\cite{lugmayr2022repaint}, to promote high-level content consistency.
elements.id-string-69: The harmonization resampling consists of incorporating backward steps $J$ in the forward diffusion process, to bring information from future more refined steps back to earlier steps.
elements.id-string-70: This is achieved by resampling $x_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{1-\beta_t} x_{t-1}, \beta_t \mathbb{1})$ for a fixed number of steps, and restarting the diffusion from that iteration.

elements.id-string-122: We derive a novel fuzzy-conditioned image diffusion capable of generating random images with pixel-wise varying degrees of image conditioning.
elements.id-string-123: We also present a diffusion projection attention that creates an anomaly detection map.
elements.id-string-124: We use this map as fuzzy guidance to our conditioned diffusion and show how it can autonomously correct facial images.
elements.id-string-125: We note that our application is trained on faces, and a flexible learning for scale adjustment would be needed to extend to other domains.
elements.id-string-126: Future work can also explore a frequency/latent-domain version of our method, for non-spatially-defined conditioning.
